cau_hoi: In which country today is the ancient city of Rome located?
giai_thich: Rome is the capital of Italy today. From a small settlement by the Tiber River, Rome grew to become the center of the Roman Empire, which once stretched from England to Egypt. Hence the saying, "All roads lead to Rome."

cau_hoi: In which city is the famous Roman Colosseum located?
giai_thich: The Colosseum was built in Rome and inaugurated in 80 AD under Emperor Titus. The arena could hold about 50,000 spectators and was the site of gladiatorial contests and wild animal hunts. Today, it is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

cau_hoi: The ancient Olympic Games originated from which country?
giai_thich: The ancient Olympics were held at Olympia, Greece, recorded as starting in 776 BC, every four years to honor the god Zeus. The modern Olympics were revived by Pierre de Coubertin (a Frenchman) in 1896, with the first modern games also taking place in Greece, in the capital Athens.

cau_hoi: Which French emperor was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815?
giai_thich: Napoléon was defeated by the British coalition (led by the Duke of Wellington) and the Prussians (led by Blücher) at Waterloo, now in Belgium, on June 18, 1815. After this battle, he was exiled to the island of Saint Helena. To this day, "to meet one's Waterloo" remains an English idiom for a final defeat.

cau_hoi: The Berlin Wall once divided the city of Berlin in which country?
giai_thich: After World War II, Germany and the city of Berlin were divided. In 1961, East Germany built the Berlin Wall to prevent people from fleeing to West Berlin. The wall fell in 1989, paving the way for German reunification in 1990.

cau_hoi: What were the seafaring warriors from Northern Europe who raided Europe during the Middle Ages called?
giai_thich: The Vikings came from the Scandinavian region (present-day Norway, Sweden, and Denmark). They built long, lightweight ships that could navigate both the sea and rivers. The Vikings not only raided but also traded and settled in various places, from England and Iceland to Russia and North America.

cau_hoi: Which city is considered the cradle of ancient democracy?
giai_thich: Athens is regarded as the cradle of democracy because, from the 5th century BC, adult male citizens could directly meet and vote on major issues of the city-state. Women, slaves, and foreigners did not have this right. The term "democracy" also originates from Greek, meaning "power of the people."

cau_hoi: What famous ship sank in 1912 after hitting an iceberg?
giai_thich: The Titanic was the largest passenger ship of its time, advertised as "unsinkable." On the night of April 14 to 15, 1912, the ship struck an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank, resulting in over 1,500 deaths. One reason was that the ship did not have enough lifeboats for everyone.

cau_hoi: In what year did World War I begin?
giai_thich: World War I began in 1914, following the assassination of the Austro-Hungarian Archduke in Sarajevo, and ended in 1918. This was the first war to use airplanes, tanks, and poison gas on a large scale, resulting in millions of deaths.

cau_hoi: Which queen had the longest reign in British history?
giai_thich: Elizabeth II ascended to the throne in 1952 at the age of 25 and reigned for 70 years until her death in 2022. She surpassed the record of Queen Victoria (about 63 years). Her successor is her eldest son, King Charles III.

cau_hoi: Which artist painted the "Mona Lisa"?
giai_thich: Leonardo da Vinci was a genius of the Italian Renaissance, being both a painter and an inventor, engineer, and anatomist. He painted the Mona Lisa in the early 16th century. The painting is famous for its mysterious smile and is now displayed at the Louvre Museum in Paris. Michelangelo and Raphael were also renowned Renaissance artists but did not paint this work.

cau_hoi: According to legend, which city did the Greek army hide in a giant wooden horse to infiltrate?
giai_thich: According to mythology, the Greek army besieged the city of Troy for 10 years without success. They pretended to retreat, leaving behind a giant wooden horse with soldiers hidden inside. The Trojans brought the horse into the city, and at night, the Greek soldiers opened the gates. Today, the "Trojan horse" is also the name of a type of computer virus.

cau_hoi: When did World War II in Europe end?
giai_thich: Nazi Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8, 1945, now known as Victory in Europe Day. In Asia, World War II ended later, when Japan surrendered in August 1945. The war began in 1939.

cau_hoi: The Bastille prison was attacked by the people in 1789, marking the beginning of which revolution?
giai_thich: The Bastille was a fortress and prison in Paris, symbolizing the king's oppressive power. On July 14, 1789, the people of Paris attacked and captured the Bastille, marking the beginning of the French Revolution. July 14 is now celebrated as Bastille Day in France.

cau_hoi: King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table are legends from which country?
giai_thich: King Arthur is a legendary figure from England and Wales. He pulled the sword Excalibur and sat with the knights around the Round Table, so no one would sit at the "head of the table" and everyone was equal. Historians are still unsure whether King Arthur was a real person.

cau_hoi: Which kingdom was Alexander the Great king of?
giai_thich: Alexander became king of Macedonia (north of Greece) in 336 BC at the age of 20. In just about 13 years, he conquered the Persian Empire, Egypt, and advanced as far as India. He died in 323 BC in Babylon at the age of 32, having never lost a major battle.

cau_hoi: In which city was Julius Caesar assassinated in 44 BC?
giai_thich: Julius Caesar was stabbed to death by a group of senators, including Brutus and Cassius, in Rome on the Ides of March (March 15) in 44 BC. They feared Caesar would become king and end the Republic. Ironically, after his death, Rome transitioned to an imperial system.

cau_hoi: Which kingdom sponsored Christopher Columbus's voyage in 1492?
giai_thich: Columbus was from Genoa (Italy), but Portugal refused to help him. Ultimately, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain sponsored his voyage in 1492. Columbus aimed to sail west to reach Asia but ended up in the Americas. He believed until his death that he had reached India, which is why the natives were called "Indians."

cau_hoi: Which volcano buried the city of Pompeii in 79 AD?
giai_thich: In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius near Naples (Italy) erupted, burying the city of Pompeii under several meters of ash. The ash preserved homes, murals, and even the shapes of the people at that time. Thus, Pompeii is a "time machine" that helps us understand Roman life. Etna is another volcano located on the island of Sicily.

cau_hoi: Who was the Prime Minister of the UK leading the country for most of World War II?
giai_thich: Winston Churchill became Prime Minister of the UK in May 1940, just as Germany attacked France. He is famous for his inspiring speeches, such as "We shall never surrender." Neville Chamberlain was the previous Prime Minister, who followed a policy of appeasement towards Hitler. Churchill also won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

cau_hoi: What did the Romans call the land now known as France?
giai_thich: The Romans referred to the land now known as France and Belgium as Gaul (Latin: Gallia). Julius Caesar conquered Gaul between 58 and 50 BC and wrote the book "The Gallic Wars" recounting it. Britannia is England, Hispania is the Iberian Peninsula, and Germania is the land of the Germans.

cau_hoi: What is ancient Sparta most famous for?
giai_thich: Sparta was the strongest military city-state in Greece. Boys left their families at the age of 7 to enter a military training school called agoge, where they learned to endure hunger, cold, and combat. Athens, on the other hand, was famous for philosophy, art, and maritime trade.

cau_hoi: In which century did the "Black Death" devastate Europe?
giai_thich: "The Black Death" was a plague pandemic caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, transmitted through fleas living on rats. The outbreak peaked from 1347 to 1351 (14th century), killing about one-third of Europe's population. After the pandemic, due to a labor shortage, peasants demanded higher wages, leading to changes in feudal society.

cau_hoi: In what year was the NATO military alliance established?
giai_thich: NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was established on April 4, 1949, in Washington, with 12 original members. Its purpose was for member countries to mutually defend each other against the Soviet Union during the Cold War. The most famous principle is "an attack on one is an attack on all." 1955 was the year the Soviet Union established the Warsaw Pact.

cau_hoi: Which English king was limited in power by the "Magna Carta" in 1215?
giai_thich: King John of England lost battles, imposed heavy taxes, and faced rebellion from the barons. In 1215, at Runnymede, he was forced to seal the Magna Carta (Great Charter), a document stating that even the king must follow the law. This document influenced the constitutions of many countries later, including the United States.

cau_hoi: In 1066, which battle did William of Normandy conquer England?
giai_thich: On October 14, 1066, William, Duke of Normandy (France), defeated King Harold II of England at Hastings. Harold was killed, reportedly by an arrow to the eye. William ascended to the throne, known as "William the Conqueror." As a result, English absorbed many words from French.

cau_hoi: How many wives did King Henry VIII of England have?
giai_thich: Henry VIII married 6 wives. English students remember their fates through the phrase "divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived." Because he wanted to divorce his first wife, which the Pope did not allow, he separated England from the Roman Catholic Church and established the Church of England.

cau_hoi: Who invented the movable type printing press in Europe around 1440?
giai_thich: Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz (Germany) invented the printing press using movable metal type that could be rearranged, around 1440. The Gutenberg Bible was printed around 1455. Thanks to the printing press, books became cheaper and knowledge spread faster than ever before. This laid the groundwork for the Renaissance and the Protestant Reformation.

cau_hoi: What movement did Martin Luther initiate in 1517?
giai_thich: In 1517, monk Martin Luther published 95 theses in Wittenberg (Germany), opposing the Church's sale of "indulgences." His movement led to the birth of Protestantism, separating from the Catholic Church. Thanks to Gutenberg's printing press, Luther's ideas spread across Europe in just a few weeks.

cau_hoi: In what year did the Soviet Union dissolve?
giai_thich: The Soviet Union consisted of 15 republics and officially dissolved in December 1991. This led to the emergence of 15 independent countries, the largest of which is Russia. 1989 was the year the Berlin Wall fell, occurring before the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

cau_hoi: In what year was the Spanish Armada defeated while attempting to attack England?
giai_thich: In 1588, King Philip II of Spain sent the Armada fleet of about 130 ships to attack England under Queen Elizabeth I. The English fleet used fire ships to break the formation. Subsequently, many Spanish ships were sunk by storms. This victory helped England gradually become a maritime power.

cau_hoi: What is the Eastern Roman Empire also known as?
giai_thich: When the Roman Empire was divided, the eastern half lasted nearly 1000 more years with its capital at Constantinople, and historians refer to it as the Byzantine Empire. The people of the empire still called themselves 'Romans.' The Holy Roman Empire was a different state in Central Europe, mainly in German territories.

cau_hoi: Which treaty in 1919 officially ended World War I with Germany?
giai_thich: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, exactly 5 years after the assassination in Sarajevo. Germany was forced to accept responsibility for the war, lose territory, and pay large reparations. Discontent with this treaty later helped Hitler rise to power.

cau_hoi: In which city did the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary occur in 1914?
giai_thich: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary and his wife were shot dead by Gavrilo Princip, a young Serb from Bosnia, in Sarajevo. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Due to the tangled alliance systems, all of Europe was drawn into war within weeks.

cau_hoi: Who commanded the British fleet in the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805?
giai_thich: On October 21, 1805, near Cape Trafalgar (Spain), Admiral Horatio Nelson commanded the British fleet to defeat the French-Spanish fleet. Nelson was shot and died during the battle. This victory ensured that Napoleon would never invade England. Nelson's statue now stands on a tall column in Trafalgar Square, London.

cau_hoi: On D-Day (June 6, 1944), Allied forces landed in which region of France?
giai_thich: On June 6, 1944, approximately 156,000 American, British, Canadian, and Allied troops landed on 5 beaches in Normandy, northern France. This was the largest amphibious invasion in history, codenamed Operation Overlord. The Germans believed the landing would occur at Calais, which is closer to England.

cau_hoi: In what year was Charlemagne crowned Emperor by the Pope?
giai_thich: On Christmas Day in 800, Pope Leo III placed the crown on Charlemagne, the king of the Franks, in Rome and proclaimed him 'Emperor of the Romans.' This was the first time the West had an emperor since the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476. Charlemagne is considered the 'Father of Europe.'

cau_hoi: In what year did the Western Roman Empire fall?
giai_thich: In 476, the German leader Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor of the Western Roman Empire, who was only about 16 years old at the time. Historians consider this the end of antiquity and the beginning of the Middle Ages in Europe. The year 1453 marks the fall of the Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine).

cau_hoi: In 1453, which empire captured the city of Constantinople?
giai_thich: Sultan Mehmed II of the Ottoman Empire besieged Constantinople with massive cannons and captured the city on May 29, 1453. The city became the capital of the Ottomans and later was named Istanbul. Many Greek scholars fled to Italy with ancient books, contributing to the Renaissance.

cau_hoi: The Hundred Years' War was fought between which two countries?
giai_thich: The Hundred Years' War between England and France lasted from 1337 to 1453, a total of 116 years. In fact, it was a series of battles interspersed with periods of truce. The main cause was the English kings' claim to the French throne. Ultimately, England lost almost all its territories in France, retaining only Calais.

cau_hoi: Which country did the heroine Jeanne d'Arc (Joan of Arc) fight for?
giai_thich: Jeanne d'Arc was a French peasant girl who believed she was guided by saints to save France. In 1429, at the age of 17, she helped the French army lift the siege of Orléans. Later, she was captured and executed by the English in 1431, and was canonized by the Church in 1920.

cau_hoi: In which country did the Renaissance begin?
giai_thich: The Renaissance means "rebirth", referring to the revival of ancient Greek and Roman culture. The movement began in Florence (Italy) in the 14th – 15th centuries, thanks to wealthy trading cities and artistic patronage from families like the Medici. The Renaissance later spread to France, England, and the Netherlands.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the trade alliance of North German cities during the Middle Ages?
giai_thich: The Hanseatic League was an alliance of trading cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen. The league controlled the trade of fish, timber, furs, and grain in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea from the 13th to the 15th centuries. To this day, Hamburg still calls itself the "Hanseatic City", and its license plates start with the letters HH.

cau_hoi: Which city-state led the Delos League in ancient Greece?
giai_thich: After defeating the Persians, in 478 BC, the Greek city-states formed the Delos League for mutual defense, led by Athens. The treasury was initially located on the island of Delos. Gradually, Athens transformed the alliance into its own "empire", even using common funds to build the Parthenon. This caused concern for Sparta and led to the Peloponnesian War.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Marathon in 490 BC, which army did the Greeks defeat?
giai_thich: In 490 BC, the Athenians defeated a larger Persian army on the plains of Marathon. Legend has it that the soldier Pheidippides ran about 40 km to Athens to announce the victory and then collapsed and died. The marathon race today (42.195 km) is named after this story.

cau_hoi: The Peloponnesian War (431 – 404 BC) was a conflict between which two sides?
giai_thich: The Peloponnesian War (431 – 404 BC) was a conflict between Athens, strong in naval power, and Sparta, strong in infantry. Athens also suffered from a major plague that killed many, including the leader Pericles. Sparta won, but both Greece weakened, creating an opportunity for Macedonia to rise later.

cau_hoi: Which general led war elephants across which mountain range to attack Rome?
giai_thich: In 218 BC, the Carthaginian general Hannibal led an army with about 37 war elephants from Spain across the Pyrenees and then over the Alps to invade Italy. Many soldiers and nearly all the elephants died from the cold. The Romans were not expecting the enemy to attack from the high northern mountains.

cau_hoi: Which city-state did General Hannibal serve?
giai_thich: Carthage was a city founded by the Phoenicians in North Africa, now part of Tunisia. It was a maritime trade power and Rome's greatest rival. Hannibal was sworn by his father from a young age to be a lifelong enemy of Rome.

cau_hoi: Who was the first emperor of Rome?
giai_thich: Julius Caesar held absolute power but only referred to himself as "dictator for life", not emperor. His grandnephew and adopted son Octavian was granted the title Augustus by the Senate in 27 BC and became the first emperor. The month of August in English is named after him, while July is named after Julius Caesar.

cau_hoi: Which Roman emperor ordered the construction of a wall across northern England?
giai_thich: Emperor Hadrian ordered the construction of a stone wall about 117 km long across northern England starting in 122 AD. The wall marked the empire's border and prevented northern tribes (now Scotland) from invading. Today, the wall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cau_hoi: Which Roman emperor granted religious freedom to Christians through the Edict of Milan in 313?
giai_thich: Previously, Christians were persecuted by Rome, such as during the times of Nero and Diocletian. In 313, Constantine and co-emperor Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, allowing everyone to freely practice their religion. By 380, under Theodosius, Christianity became the state religion of Rome.

cau_hoi: In which year did Pope Urban II call for the First Crusade?
giai_thich: In 1095, the Byzantine emperor requested help from the West against the Seljuk Turks. Pope Urban II then called for the Crusade at the Council of Clermont (France). The Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099. The year 1066 was when the Battle of Hastings occurred, and 1187 was when Saladin recaptured Jerusalem.

cau_hoi: Which Crusade did King Richard the Lionheart of England participate in?
giai_thich: The Third Crusade (1189 – 1192) broke out after Saladin recaptured Jerusalem. King Richard the Lionheart of England won many battles but did not reclaim Jerusalem. He only managed to secure an agreement for Christian pilgrims to enter the city. On his way back, Richard was captured and had to pay a huge ransom.

cau_hoi: Which wealthy family is famous for patronizing the arts in Florence during the Renaissance?
giai_thich: The Medici family became wealthy through banking and nearly ruled Florence for many generations. They patronized artists such as Botticelli, Michelangelo, and scientist Galileo. This family also had four members become popes and two who became queens of France.

cau_hoi: Which famous chapel ceiling did Michelangelo paint?
giai_thich: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican over four years (1508 – 1512), often having to stand on scaffolding and tilt his head back to paint. The most famous part is "The Creation of Adam," where two fingers nearly touch. Michelangelo considered himself a sculptor rather than a painter.

cau_hoi: Which maritime explorer was the first European to sail around Africa to reach India?
giai_thich: Vasco da Gama (Portugal) sailed around the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa and reached Calicut, India in 1498. This sea route allowed Europe to buy pepper and spices without going through Arab intermediaries. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope earlier in 1488 but did not reach India.

cau_hoi: Whose expedition was the first to circumnavigate the globe (1519 – 1522)?
giai_thich: Magellan (a Portuguese serving Spain) set sail in 1519 with five ships and about 270 men. He was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the only remaining ship, Victoria, back to Spain in 1522, with only 18 survivors. The voyage proved that the Earth is round and larger than previously thought.

cau_hoi: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
giai_thich: The Industrial Revolution began in England in the late 18th century. England had abundant coal and iron, colonies providing raw materials and markets, and many inventors. Steam-powered machines replaced human labor, textile mills sprang up, and people flocked to cities for work.

cau_hoi: Who improved the steam engine, contributing to the Industrial Revolution?
giai_thich: James Watt (Scottish) did not invent the first steam engine. He improved the Newcomen engine by adding a separate condenser (patented in 1769), which greatly saved fuel. The unit of power "watt" is named after him. George Stephenson was the famous locomotive builder later on.

cau_hoi: "La Marseillaise" is the national anthem of which country?
giai_thich: "La Marseillaise" was composed by Rouget de Lisle in 1792 as a marching song for the army. The song became famous when volunteers from Marseille sang it while entering Paris, hence the name. In 1795, it became the national anthem of France. Belgium and Switzerland also speak French but have their own anthems.

cau_hoi: In what year was King Louis XVI of France executed?
giai_thich: After the monarchy was abolished in 1792, King Louis XVI was tried for treason and executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793. Queen Marie Antoinette was also executed in October of the same year. The year 1789 marks the beginning of the revolution, when the king was still on the throne.

cau_hoi: Where was Napoleon finally exiled and died?
giai_thich: After his defeat at Waterloo, the British exiled Napoleon to the remote island of Saint Helena, located nearly 2,000 km from Africa in the South Atlantic, to prevent him from escaping again. He died there in 1821. Elba (near Italy) was where he was first exiled in 1814 and managed to escape.

cau_hoi: On which island was Napoleon Bonaparte born?
giai_thich: Napoleon was born on August 15, 1769, in Ajaccio on the island of Corsica. Just a year earlier, in 1768, Corsica had been ceded to France by the Republic of Genoa. Therefore, his native language was Corsican (similar to Italian), and when he studied in France, he spoke French with difficulty.

cau_hoi: In what year did the Russian October Revolution take place?
giai_thich: In October according to the old Julian calendar of Russia (November 1917 in the current calendar), the Bolshevik Party led by Lenin seized the Winter Palace in Petrograd and overthrew the Provisional Government. This was the first successful socialist revolution in the world. The Soviet Union was officially established in 1922.

cau_hoi: Who led the Russian October Revolution?
giai_thich: Vladimir Lenin was the leader of the Bolshevik Party and the founder of the Soviet state. He led the October Revolution in 1917. After Lenin's death in 1924, Stalin gradually took power. Gorbachev and Khrushchev were Soviet leaders in later periods.

cau_hoi: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
giai_thich: Nicholas II was the last Tsar of the Romanov dynasty. He abdicated in March 1917 amid war, famine, and widespread protests. In 1918, he and his family were executed by the Bolsheviks in Yekaterinburg. Peter the Great and Ivan the Terrible were famous tsars from many centuries earlier.

cau_hoi: Which three countries' leaders participated in the Yalta Conference in 1945?
giai_thich: In February 1945, the three leaders Churchill (Britain), Roosevelt (USA), and Stalin (Soviet Union), known as the "Big Three," met in Yalta on the Crimean Peninsula. They discussed the division of Germany into occupation zones and the establishment of the United Nations. France and China did not participate in this conference.

cau_hoi: In what year did the Berlin Wall fall?
giai_thich: On the evening of November 9, 1989, the East German government announced that citizens could cross the border. Thousands rushed to the checkpoints, and people on both sides began to break down the wall with hammers. This event symbolized the end of the Cold War in Europe. Germany was reunified a year later, in 1990.

cau_hoi: In what year were euro banknotes and coins introduced?
giai_thich: The euro was introduced on January 1, 1999, but initially only used for banking and electronic transfers. Euro banknotes and coins were put into circulation on January 1, 2002, replacing currencies like the French franc and the German mark. Today, about 20 countries use the euro.

cau_hoi: Which battle (1942 – 1943) is considered a turning point on the Eastern Front in World War II?
giai_thich: From the summer of 1942 to February 1943, German forces attacked Stalingrad (now Volgograd), a city named after Stalin on the Volga River. The Soviet Red Army counterattacked and encircled the entire German Sixth Army, forcing about 90,000 German soldiers to surrender. From then on, Germany gradually shifted to a defensive position. El Alamein was a British victory in North Africa around the same time.

cau_hoi: Who is known as the "Iron Chancellor", the person who unified Germany in 1871?
giai_thich: Otto von Bismarck was the Chancellor of Prussia. He stated that the great issues of the era would be resolved "by iron and blood" rather than by speeches. After three wars against Denmark, Austria, and France, he unified the German states into the German Empire in 1871. Metternich was an Austrian statesman from the previous era.

cau_hoi: Which philosopher was the teacher of Alexander the Great?
giai_thich: Aristotle was a student of Plato, who was in turn a student of Socrates. King Philip II of Macedonia invited Aristotle to teach his son Alexander around 343 BC when he was 13 years old. It is said that Alexander carried a copy of the Iliad annotated by Aristotle throughout his conquests.

cau_hoi: How was the philosopher Socrates executed?
giai_thich: In 399 BC, Socrates was convicted by the Athenian court of "not believing in the gods of the city" and "corrupting the youth" for frequently questioning people. He was allowed to escape but refused, and drank a cup of poison hemlock to comply with the sentence. Socrates did not write books. We mainly know about him through the works of his student Plato.

cau_hoi: Which Spartan king led 300 warriors at the Battle of Thermopylae in 480 BC?
giai_thich: In 480 BC, King Leonidas of Sparta, along with 300 Spartan warriors and a few thousand allied troops, blocked the massive army of Persian King Xerxes at the narrow pass of Thermopylae. They held out for 3 days until betrayed: a local revealed a path around the mountains to the Persian forces. All sacrificed themselves, becoming a symbol of courage.

cau_hoi: Which Athenian leader commissioned the construction of the Parthenon during the Golden Age?
giai_thich: Pericles was the leader of Athens during its Golden Age (around 461 – 429 BC). He used the treasury of the Delian League to rebuild the Acropolis, including the Parthenon dedicated to the goddess Athena, starting in 447 BC. This era is also known as the "Age of Pericles."

cau_hoi: What are the three wars between Rome and Carthage called?
giai_thich: "Punic" comes from the Latin word "Punicus", meaning Phoenician, as Carthage was founded by Phoenicians. Rome and Carthage fought three times from 264 to 146 BC for control of the Mediterranean. At the end of the third war, Carthage was completely destroyed.

cau_hoi: Which river did Julius Caesar cross in 49 BC, associated with the phrase "The die is cast"?
giai_thich: The Rubicon River was the boundary between the province of Gaul governed by Caesar and Italy. Roman law prohibited generals from leading troops across the river into Italy. In 49 BC, Caesar crossed the river and is said to have declared "The die is cast", meaning there was no turning back. To this day, "crossing the Rubicon" is an idiom for making an irreversible decision.

cau_hoi: Which Egyptian queen was an ally of Julius Caesar and Mark Antony?
giai_thich: Cleopatra VII belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from a Greek general of Alexander the Great, so she was actually of Greek origin rather than Egyptian. She was the last pharaoh of Egypt, allied with Caesar and then with Mark Antony. After their defeat at Actium, she committed suicide in 30 BC, and Egypt became a province of Rome.

cau_hoi: Which queen of the Iceni tribe led a revolt against Rome in Britain around 60 – 61?
giai_thich: Boudica was the queen of the Iceni tribe in eastern England. Around 60 – 61, after being mistreated by the Romans, she led a revolt and burned down three cities, including Londinium (modern-day London). Ultimately, she was defeated by Roman forces. Today, there is a statue of her riding a chariot near the UK Parliament.

cau_hoi: Which leader of the Huns attacked the Roman Empire in the 5th century?
giai_thich: Attila led the Huns, a nomadic cavalry people from the Asian steppes, around 434 – 453. He attacked both Eastern and Western Rome, causing the Romans to call him "The Scourge of God". In 452, he invaded Italy but withdrew after meeting Pope Leo I. Genghis Khan lived about 750 years later.

cau_hoi: In 410, the city of Rome was sacked by the Visigoths under the command of whom?
giai_thich: In 410, the Visigoth army led by King Alaric captured and plundered Rome for three days. This was the first time in about 800 years that Rome fell into enemy hands, shocking the entire Roman world. This event signaled the decline of the Western Roman Empire, just 66 years before its collapse in 476.

cau_hoi: Which Byzantine emperor commissioned the construction of the Hagia Sophia (the current structure) in 537?
giai_thich: Emperor Justinian I rebuilt the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople in just about 5 years, completing it in 537. The massive dome of the church was the largest dome in the world for nearly 1000 years. After 1453, the structure was converted into a mosque, and minarets were added.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the Roman law code compiled during Justinian's reign?
giai_thich: Corpus Juris Civilis (Body of Civil Law) is the compilation of Roman law commissioned by Justinian between 529 and 534. This code was rediscovered by the West in the 11th century and became the foundation of civil law systems in France, Germany, and many other countries. The Twelve Tables is a much older Roman law code, dating back to around 450 BC.

cau_hoi: What event occurred in 1054 between the Western and Eastern Churches?
giai_thich: In 1054, the Western Church (Rome, speaking Latin) and the Eastern Church (Constantinople, speaking Greek) disagreed over the authority of the Pope and various rituals. Both sides excommunicated each other. From then on, Christianity split into Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy, and this division remains to this day.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the land and property survey book created in England by William the Conqueror in 1086?
giai_thich: In 1086, William the Conqueror sent people throughout England to record who owned land, how many livestock there were, and mills for tax purposes. The people referred to this book as "Domesday" (Day of Judgment), because what was recorded in it was indisputable. This is one of the oldest surviving statistical documents in Europe.

cau_hoi: What famous embroidered tapestry depicts the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
giai_thich: The Bayeux Tapestry is nearly 70 meters long and was hand-stitched in the 11th century. In fact, it is a wool embroidery on linen. The tapestry tells the story of the conquest of England in 1066 through about 50 scenes, resembling a medieval comic book. It even depicts Halley's Comet appearing in 1066.

cau_hoi: Which city was sacked during the Fourth Crusade (1204)?
giai_thich: In 1204, the army of the Fourth Crusade ran out of money to pay Venice, which had rented them ships. Instead of going to Jerusalem or Egypt, they turned to attack and plunder Constantinople, a Christian city. Four bronze horses taken from Constantinople still remain in Venice today.

cau_hoi: Which Muslim sultan recaptured Jerusalem in 1187?
giai_thich: Saladin was the sultan of Egypt and Syria, of Kurdish descent. In 1187, he defeated the Crusader army at Hattin and then recaptured Jerusalem. He is famous for his chivalry, as he did not massacre the inhabitants of the city. Even enemies like Richard the Lionheart respected him.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Agincourt in 1415, archers from which country achieved victory?
giai_thich: In 1415, King Henry V's English army, tired and hungry, defeated the much larger French army at Agincourt. English archers used longbows to rain arrows on the French cavalry, which was bogged down in the muddy fields. This battle is recounted by Shakespeare in the play "Henry V."

cau_hoi: What is the name of the 15th-century civil war in England between the houses of York and Lancaster?
giai_thich: The Wars of the Roses (1455 – 1487) were a struggle for the throne between two branches of the Plantagenet dynasty: the Yorks, symbolized by the white rose, and the Lancasters, represented by the red rose. Henry Tudor won the Battle of Bosworth in 1485 and then married Elizabeth of York to reconcile the factions. The series "Game of Thrones" is partially inspired by this conflict.

cau_hoi: Which dynasty in England began with King Henry VII after the Wars of the Roses?
giai_thich: Henry VII ascended to the throne in 1485, founding the Tudor dynasty. The symbol of the Tudor house is the combined red and white rose. Notable Tudor monarchs include Henry VIII and Elizabeth I. When Elizabeth I died in 1603 without an heir, the throne passed to the Stuart dynasty from Scotland.

cau_hoi: Who is the author of the "Divine Comedy"?
giai_thich: Dante Alighieri (Florence) wrote the "Divine Comedy" in the early 14th century, narrating an imaginary journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise. He wrote in the Tuscan vernacular instead of Latin, helping to shape standard Italian. Thus, Dante is often referred to as the "Father of the Italian Language."

cau_hoi: Who wrote the political book "The Prince"?
giai_thich: Niccolò Machiavelli was a diplomat from Florence. He wrote "The Prince" in 1513, advising rulers on when to be lenient and when to be ruthless to maintain power. This led to the term "Machiavellian," which denotes cunning and political scheming. Thomas More (England) wrote "Utopia" about an ideal society.

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided new lands between which two countries?
giai_thich: After Columbus's voyage, Spain and Portugal competed for new lands. In 1494, the two countries signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, drawing a meridian line to divide the world: lands to the west belonged to Spain, and those to the east to Portugal. The eastern tip of South America fell under Portuguese control, which is why Brazil today speaks Portuguese.

cau_hoi: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Aztec Empire?
giai_thich: In 1519, Hernán Cortés arrived in Mexico with only about 500 soldiers. He allied with tribes that hated the Aztecs and was supported by guns, horses, and smallpox brought by Europeans. By 1521, he captured the capital Tenochtitlan, now Mexico City.

cau_hoi: Which Spanish conquistador conquered the Inca Empire?
giai_thich: Francisco Pizarro arrived in Peru in 1532 with fewer than 200 men. He took advantage of the Inca Empire's recent civil war, captured King Atahualpa, and demanded a room full of gold as ransom but still executed the king. The Inca city of Machu Picchu was fortunate to remain undiscovered by the Spanish.

cau_hoi: The Gunpowder Plot of 1605 by Guy Fawkes aimed to blow up which building?
giai_thich: Guy Fawkes and a group of Catholics hid 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath the Houses of Parliament, planning to blow it up on the day King James I was to open the session on November 5, 1605. The plot was discovered, and Fawkes was caught right next to the gunpowder. The English still light bonfires and set off fireworks on "Guy Fawkes Night" every year.

cau_hoi: The Great Fire of London occurred in which year?
giai_thich: In September 1666, a fire broke out from a bakery on Pudding Lane. Due to closely packed wooden houses and strong winds, the fire spread for four days, destroying about 13,000 homes and the old St. Paul's Cathedral. London was then rebuilt in brick and stone, and architect Christopher Wren reconstructed St. Paul's Cathedral as we see it today.

cau_hoi: Which French king is known as the "Sun King"?
giai_thich: Louis XIV ascended to the throne in 1643 at the age of four and reigned for 72 years, the longest of any European monarch. He chose the sun as his symbol, as if everything in the country revolved around him. He is said to have declared, "L'état, c'est moi" (I am the state). Louis XVI, who was executed during the French Revolution, was his great-great-grandson.

cau_hoi: From 1682, Louis XIV moved the court to which palace?
giai_thich: Louis XIV transformed a hunting lodge in Versailles into a magnificent palace and moved the court there in 1682. He required the nobility to live in the palace to better control them. The famous Hall of Mirrors contains 357 mirrors. This is also where the Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919.

cau_hoi: Which Greek historian is known as the "Father of History"?
giai_thich: Herodotus (circa 484 – 425 BC) wrote the "Histories" (Historiai) recounting the wars between Greece and Persia. He was the first to travel extensively to gather materials and investigate the causes of events, earning him the title "Father of History" from the Roman orator Cicero. Thucydides, who wrote about the Peloponnesian War, is known for a more rigorous approach to historical writing.

cau_hoi: To whom are the epic poems "Iliad" and "Odyssey" attributed?
giai_thich: The Iliad tells the story of the final days of the Trojan War, focusing on the wrath of the hero Achilles. The Odyssey narrates Odysseus's ten-year journey home. Both are attributed to the poet Homer (circa 8th century BC). It is said that Homer was blind, and the epics were originally passed down orally before being recorded.

cau_hoi: Who authored the Roman epic "Aeneid"?
giai_thich: Virgil wrote the "Aeneid" at the request of Emperor Augustus, telling the story of Aeneas, a Trojan prince who escapes the fall of Troy and travels to Italy. Aeneas's descendants are said to have founded Rome. This epic provided the Romans with a heroic "ancestor" on par with the Greek heroes of Homer.

cau_hoi: Which reformer is considered the father of Athenian democracy (around 508 BC)?
giai_thich: Around 508 BC, Cleisthenes reformed Athens by dividing citizens into 10 new tribes based on residence rather than lineage. This approach broke the power of noble families. He also established the Council of 500. Solon was an earlier reformer who abolished debt slavery.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Actium in 31 BC, whom did Octavian defeat?
giai_thich: After Caesar's assassination, Octavian and Mark Antony vied for power. In 31 BC, Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium, off the coast of Greece. A year later, both committed suicide. Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome and received the title Augustus in 27 BC.

cau_hoi: In which year did Emperor Constantine officially move the capital to Constantinople?
giai_thich: Constantine built the new capital on the site of the ancient city of Byzantium, strategically located between Europe and Asia, controlling the Bosphorus Strait. He officially inaugurated the city in 330 and named it "New Rome," later known as Constantinople. The year 313 marks the Edict of Milan, while 395 is when the empire permanently split.

cau_hoi: In 395, the Roman Empire permanently split into East and West after the death of which emperor?
giai_thich: Theodosius I was the last emperor to rule both Eastern and Western Rome. Upon his death in 395, his two sons divided the empire: Arcadius ruled the east (Constantinople), and Honorius ruled the west. From then on, the empire was never unified again. Theodosius also made Christianity the state religion in 380.

cau_hoi: Which Roman emperor established the "Tetrarchy" (rule by four)?
giai_thich: The empire was too vast for one person to govern, so in 293 Diocletian established the Tetrarchy: two senior emperors (Augusti) and two junior emperors (Caesars), each responsible for a region. This system quickly fell apart after his abdication. Diocletian was the first Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate, returning to his homeland to grow cabbages.

cau_hoi: Which emperor-philosopher of Rome wrote the book "Meditations"?
giai_thich: Marcus Aurelius ruled from 161 to 180 and followed the Stoic philosophical school. This school teaches individuals to remain calm and focus only on what they can control. He wrote "Meditations" in Greek as a personal diary while campaigning on the frontiers. Today, the book is still widely read.

cau_hoi: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest extent (in 117)?
giai_thich: Trajan (reigned 98 – 117) was the first emperor born outside Italy, in Hispania (modern-day Spain). He conquered Dacia (Romania) and Mesopotamia, expanding the empire to its largest size, approximately 5 million square kilometers. The Trajan's Column in Rome depicts scenes of the Dacian Wars in a spiraling relief. His successor Hadrian later withdrew to secure the borders.

cau_hoi: What is the name of Charlemagne's dynasty?
giai_thich: The name Carolingian comes from "Carolus", the Latin name for Charles, named after Charles Martel and Charlemagne (Charles the Great). This dynasty replaced the Merovingian dynasty in 751 when Pepin the Short (Charlemagne's father) ascended to the throne. The Carolingian period saw the "Carolingian Renaissance", a time when writing, books, and schools were revived.

cau_hoi: Which king unified the Franks and converted to Christianity in the late 5th – early 6th century?
giai_thich: Clovis I unified the Frankish tribes and defeated the last remnants of Roman power in Gaul. Traditionally, he was baptized around 496 in Reims. His conversion to Catholicism helped him gain the support of the Church and the people of Gaul. The name "Clovis" later evolved into "Louis", the name of 18 French kings.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Tours (Poitiers) in 732, which force did Charles Martel halt?
giai_thich: In 732, the Umayyad Muslim army advanced deep into France from Spain. Charles Martel, who held the real power of the Frankish kingdom, defeated them between Tours and Poitiers. He is known as "Martel" (The Hammer). He was the grandfather of Charlemagne.

cau_hoi: When did Otto I get crowned emperor, marking the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire?
giai_thich: In 962, German King Otto I was crowned emperor by the Pope in Rome. Historians consider this the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire, which primarily included the territories of Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic, and northern Italy. Philosopher Voltaire once mocked that this empire was "neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire."

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided Charlemagne's empire into how many parts?
giai_thich: After the death of Charlemagne's son Louis the Pious, three grandsons fought for the land. In 843, the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire into three parts: the west (later becoming France), the east (later becoming Germany), and the strip of land in between from the Netherlands to Italy. This central strip would become a contested area between France and Germany for centuries.

cau_hoi: Which Anglo-Saxon king fought against the Vikings and was called "the Great"?
giai_thich: Alfred (reigned 871 – 899) was the king of Wessex. He defeated the Vikings at the Battle of Edington in 878, built fortified towns, and established a navy. He also encouraged the translation of books into English. Alfred is the only English king to be called "the Great". Legend has it that he once burned a peasant woman's cakes while lost in thought.

cau_hoi: Which Viking explorer is believed to have reached North America around the year 1000?
giai_thich: Leif Erikson was the son of Erik the Red, who established a settlement in Greenland. Around the year 1000, Leif sailed west and reached an area he called Vinland. In 1960, archaeologists discovered remnants of a Viking village at L'Anse aux Meadows (Canada), proving that the Vikings reached America nearly 500 years before Columbus.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Stamford Bridge in 1066, which Norwegian king did English King Harold II defeat?
giai_thich: In September 1066, Norwegian King Harald Hardrada landed in northern England. King Harold II of England marched north rapidly and defeated him at Stamford Bridge. But just a few days later, William of Normandy landed in the south, and Harold had to march back down to Hastings, where he was killed. Thus, 1066 was the year England had three kings.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the French dynasty that began with Hugh Capet in 987?
giai_thich: Hugh Capet was elected king of France in 987 by the nobles, replacing the Carolingian dynasty. His descendants (the direct Capetians, Valois, Bourbon) ruled France until 1848, and today the king of Spain still belongs to this lineage. Therefore, during the French Revolution, King Louis XVI was referred to as "Citizen Louis Capet."

cau_hoi: The Reconquista on the Iberian Peninsula ended in 1492 with the recapture of which city?
giai_thich: Reconquista means "reconquest": the Christian kingdoms on the Iberian Peninsula gradually reclaimed land from the Muslims, lasting nearly 800 years (from 711 to 1492). Granada, with its beautiful Alhambra palace, was the last Muslim kingdom, surrendering in January 1492. The same year, Columbus set sail for America.

cau_hoi: Which country is the Habsburg dynasty originally from?
giai_thich: The Habsburg family takes its name from Habsburg Castle ("Castle of the Hawk") in Aargau, Switzerland. Later, they moved their power center to Austria and, through clever marriages, ruled Austria, Spain, the Netherlands, and many other regions. A famous saying about them is "Others wage war, but you, oh happy Austria, marry."

cau_hoi: Which war did the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 end?
giai_thich: The Thirty Years' War (1618 – 1648) began from the Catholic-Protestant conflict in the Holy Roman Empire, drawing in Sweden, France, and Spain. Many regions of Germany lost up to a third of their population. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognized the sovereignty of each nation, laying the foundation for modern international relations.

cau_hoi: Who led the Parliamentarians in the English Civil War and became the "Lord Protector"?
giai_thich: Oliver Cromwell was a landowner who became the military leader of the Parliamentarians with the "New Model Army". After King Charles I was executed, England had no king. In 1653, Cromwell became the "Lord Protector" and ruled as a dictator, even banning Christmas. Thomas Cromwell was another figure, an advisor to Henry VIII who lived about 100 years earlier.

cau_hoi: Which English king was executed in 1649?
giai_thich: Charles I believed that kings were chosen by God and did not need to listen to Parliament. This led to the English Civil War (1642 – 1651). The Parliamentarians won, tried the king for treason, and executed him in January 1649 in London. In 1660, his son Charles II was invited back to be king, marking the "Restoration" period.

cau_hoi: Which event known as the "Glorious Revolution" in 1688 brought whom to the English throne?
giai_thich: In 1688, Parliament feared that King James II, being Catholic, would become tyrannical. They invited William of Orange (from the Netherlands), the husband of Mary, James's daughter, to England. James fled to France with little fighting. William III and Mary II ascended the throne and accepted the Bill of Rights 1689, limiting the king's power.

cau_hoi: Which Tsar founded the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703?
giai_thich: Peter the Great wanted to modernize Russia in the Western style. In 1703, he built Saint Petersburg on the marshy land by the Baltic Sea, which he had just won from Sweden, and moved the capital there in 1712. He also forced nobles to shave their beards and even taxed those who had beards. He once disguised himself as a shipbuilder to learn the trade in the Netherlands.

cau_hoi: Which Austrian queen was the mother of French queen Marie Antoinette?
giai_thich: Maria Theresa was the only woman to rule the Habsburg lands (reigned 1740 – 1780). She had 16 children and married many of them into other royal families to create alliances. Her youngest daughter, Marie Antoinette, married King Louis XVI of France and was executed in 1793 during the French Revolution.

cau_hoi: Which Prussian king was known as the "Great", famous for playing the flute and composing music?
giai_thich: Frederick II (reigned 1740 – 1786) transformed Prussia into a military power through wars with Austria. He also loved the arts: he was a skilled flutist, composed over 100 pieces for the flute, and corresponded with the French philosopher Voltaire. He called himself the "first servant of the state". He also encouraged the Prussian people to grow potatoes.

cau_hoi: What is the French Civil Code of 1804 commonly known as?
giai_thich: In 1804, Napoleon enacted the Civil Code, later known as the Napoleonic Code. The code established that all citizens are equal before the law, protected private property rights, and abolished feudal privileges. The code was applied in places conquered by Napoleon and influenced the laws of many countries. Napoleon himself considered this a greater achievement than any military victory.

cau_hoi: Which victory of Napoleon in 1805 is referred to as the "Battle of the Three Emperors"?
giai_thich: On December 2, 1805, exactly one year after his coronation, Napoleon defeated the coalition of Emperor Alexander I of Russia and Emperor Francis II of Austria at Austerlitz (now in the Czech Republic). Because three emperors were involved, this battle is called the "Battle of the Three Emperors". It is considered Napoleon's greatest victory. Borodino was a major battle in 1812 in Russia.

cau_hoi: In 1812, which city in Russia did Napoleon capture but later had to retreat from?
giai_thich: In 1812, Napoleon led about 600,000 troops into Russia. The Russians retreated and burned everything in their path. After the Battle of Borodino, Napoleon entered Moscow, but the city was on fire and the Tsar refused to negotiate. On the retreat during the freezing winter, only about one-tenth of the French army survived.

cau_hoi: Which conference (1814 – 1815) redrew the map of Europe after the Napoleonic era?
giai_thich: After defeating Napoleon, the great powers of Britain, Russia, Austria, Prussia, and France met in Vienna (1814 – 1815) to redistribute territories and restore the old monarchs to the throne. Their goal was to 'balance power' so that no country became too strong. As a result, Europe avoided a major continental war until 1914.

cau_hoi: Which Austrian politician chaired the Vienna Conference?
giai_thich: Klemens von Metternich was the foreign minister and later the chancellor of Austria. He chaired the Vienna Conference and defended the old order, suppressing liberal ideas and nationalist movements for over 30 years. The revolutions of 1848 forced him to flee to England. Talleyrand was the skillful representative of France at the conference.

cau_hoi: What is the period called when Napoleon returned to power in 1815?
giai_thich: In February 1815, Napoleon escaped from Elba, landed in southern France, and was welcomed by soldiers. King Louis XVIII fled. Napoleon regained power for about 100 days (from March to July 1815) until he was defeated at Waterloo. The Second Empire refers to the time of his nephew, Napoleon III.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the bloody repression period from 1793 to 1794 during the French Revolution, associated with Robespierre?
giai_thich: During the Terror (1793 – 1794), the Committee of Public Safety led by Robespierre executed about 17,000 people deemed 'enemies of the revolution', mostly by guillotine. When even his colleagues feared being executed, they arrested Robespierre and sent him to the guillotine in July 1794. The phrase 'Revolution devours its own children' originates from this period.

cau_hoi: What is the wave of revolutions that spread across Europe in 1848 called?
giai_thich: In 1848, revolutions broke out almost simultaneously in France, the German states, Austria, Hungary, Italy, and many other places. People demanded constitutions, freedoms, and national unification. Most revolutions were suppressed within a year, but serfdom in Austria was abolished and nationalist ideas spread.

cau_hoi: Who led the 'Red Shirts' army that contributed to the unification of Italy?
giai_thich: Giuseppe Garibaldi was a freedom fighter who had fought in South America. In 1860, he and about 1,000 volunteers wearing red shirts, known as the 'Thousand', conquered Sicily and Naples. He then handed these regions over to King Victor Emmanuel II. Cavour was the shrewd prime minister who managed the unification through diplomacy.

cau_hoi: In what year was the Kingdom of Italy unified?
giai_thich: Previously, Italy was divided into many small kingdoms and territories. In 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was declared with Victor Emmanuel II as king, but Venice (annexed in 1866) and Rome (in 1870) were not yet part of Italy. Rome became the capital in 1871. The year 1871 was also the year of German unification.

cau_hoi: Where was the German Empire declared in 1871?
B: Hall of Mirrors, Palace of Versailles
giai_thich: On January 18, 1871, while the Prussian army was still besieging Paris, King Wilhelm I of Prussia was proclaimed Emperor of Germany in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. This was a great humiliation for the French. Therefore, in 1919, the French deliberately made Germany sign the Treaty of Versailles in this very room.

cau_hoi: Which famous nurse cared for British soldiers during the Crimean War (1853 – 1856)?
giai_thich: Florence Nightingale led a group of nurses to the British military hospital in Scutari (Istanbul). She improved sanitation, which significantly reduced the mortality rate. At night, she would carry a lamp to visit the wounded, earning her the nickname 'The Lady with the Lamp'. She was also skilled in statistics and used charts to persuade the government to reform. Her birthday (May 12) is now celebrated as International Nurses Day.

cau_hoi: Which country experienced the Great Famine of the mid-19th century?
giai_thich: From 1845, a type of mold caused potatoes, the staple food of the poor in Ireland, to rot. Between 1845 and 1852, about 1 million people died of starvation or disease, and around 1 to 2 million emigrated, mostly to America. To this day, Ireland's population has not returned to pre-famine levels.

cau_hoi: What issue was discussed at the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885?
giai_thich: The Berlin Conference, chaired by Bismarck (1884-1885), involved 14 countries but had no representatives from Africa. The conference established the rule that any country wanting colonies must occupy them in reality. Subsequently, European countries competed for territories, and by 1914, about 90% of Africa was under their control. Many straight borders in Africa originated from this period.

cau_hoi: In what year did Poland last get partitioned by Russia, Prussia, and Austria, disappearing from the map?
giai_thich: Poland was partitioned three times, in 1772, 1793, and 1795. After the third partition, Russia, Prussia, and Austria erased Poland from the map for 123 years. The Polish people maintained their language and culture, and the Polish national anthem begins with the line "Poland has not yet perished." Poland regained independence in 1918.

cau_hoi: Which country was part of the Central Powers alongside Germany, Austria-Hungary, and the Ottoman Empire during World War I?
giai_thich: The Central Powers included Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire (from 1914), and Bulgaria (from 1915). Although Italy had signed an alliance with Germany and Austria, it joined the Allies in 1915 due to promises of land. Romania and Serbia also fought against the Central Powers.

cau_hoi: What was the battle that lasted nearly 10 months in 1916 between France and Germany, one of the longest in history?
giai_thich: In February 1916, Germany attacked Verdun, an important French fortress, with the goal of "bleeding the French army white." The battle lasted about 10 months, resulting in approximately 700,000 casualties on both sides, but the front lines hardly changed. General Pétain commanded the defense, and the French troops vowed, "They shall not pass!".

cau_hoi: What was the name of Germany's military plan to quickly defeat France through Belgium in 1914?
giai_thich: The Schlieffen Plan aimed to avoid fighting on two fronts simultaneously: Germany would quickly defeat France within about 6 weeks by going through Belgium, then turn to fight Russia. However, the violation of Belgian neutrality led Britain to enter the war, and German forces were halted at the Marne River in September 1914. From then on, the Western Front turned into trench warfare. Operation Barbarossa pertains to World War II.

cau_hoi: Which British passenger ship was sunk by a German submarine in 1915?
giai_thich: On May 7, 1915, the German submarine U-20 torpedoed and sank the passenger ship Lusitania off the coast of Ireland. The ship sank in just 18 minutes, resulting in nearly 1,200 deaths, including 128 Americans. The incident outraged American public opinion and contributed to the U.S. entering the war in 1917. The Titanic sank after hitting an iceberg in 1912.

cau_hoi: Which treaty in 1918 allowed which country to withdraw from World War I?
giai_thich: After the October Revolution, Lenin's Bolshevik government wanted to withdraw from the war to consolidate power. In March 1918, Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany, accepting the loss of vast territories such as Poland, the Baltic states, and Ukraine. The treaty was annulled when Germany was defeated at the end of 1918.

cau_hoi: World War I armistice took effect at 11 a.m. on November 11 of which year?
giai_thich: The armistice was signed in a railway carriage in the Compiègne forest (France) at 5 a.m. and took effect at 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918. This day is now known as Armistice Day or Remembrance Day, and in the UK, people wear red poppies to honor those who fell. The Treaty of Versailles was officially signed in 1919.

cau_hoi: Which international organization was established after World War I to maintain peace?
giai_thich: The League of Nations was established in 1920 at the initiative of U.S. President Woodrow Wilson, with its headquarters in Geneva. Ironically, the United States itself did not participate. The League had no military force, so it could not prevent invasions in the 1930s and dissolved after World War II. The United Nations, founded in 1945, is its successor.

cau_hoi: Which country was Benito Mussolini a dictator of?
giai_thich: Benito Mussolini founded the Fascist Party and came to power in Italy in 1922 after the "March on Rome." He called himself "Il Duce" (The Leader) and later allied with Hitler. In 1945, he was captured and executed by Italian partisans. The term "fascist" comes from "fasces," a bundle of rods with an axe, symbolizing power in ancient Rome.

cau_hoi: Who was the dictator ruling Spain after the Civil War of 1936 – 1939?
giai_thich: General Francisco Franco led the Nationalist uprising against the Republican government in 1936. His faction was supported by Hitler and Mussolini. After three years of civil war, Franco won and ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975. Spain then became a democracy under King Juan Carlos I. Salazar was a contemporary dictator in neighboring Portugal.

cau_hoi: Which Spanish town was bombed in 1937 and became the title of a famous painting by Picasso?
giai_thich: On April 26, 1937, German and Italian planes bombed the town of Guernica in the Basque Country to assist General Franco. Hundreds of civilians were killed. Pablo Picasso painted the massive artwork "Guernica" using only three colors: black, white, and gray to protest the brutality of war. The painting is now housed in the Reina Sofía Museum in Madrid.

cau_hoi: The Munich Agreement of 1938 allowed Germany to annex which region of Czechoslovakia?
giai_thich: Sudetenland is a border region of Czechoslovakia with a significant German-speaking population. In September 1938, Britain (Chamberlain), France, Italy, and Germany met in Munich and agreed to hand over this region to Hitler without consulting Czechoslovakia. Chamberlain declared he had brought "peace for our time." Just six months later, Hitler occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia.

cau_hoi: On September 1, 1939, Germany invaded which country, marking the beginning of World War II?
giai_thich: On September 1, 1939, Germany attacked Poland using the "Blitzkrieg" (lightning war) tactic, combining tanks and aircraft. On September 3, Britain and France declared war on Germany. On September 17, the Soviet Union attacked Poland from the east under a secret agreement with Germany. Austria and Czechoslovakia had already been occupied by Germany without a war.

cau_hoi: What was the codename for Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941?
giai_thich: On June 22, 1941, about 3 million German soldiers attacked the Soviet Union, opening the largest front in history. The operation was named Barbarossa ("Red Beard"), the nickname of Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I during the Middle Ages. German forces advanced close to Moscow but were halted by winter and the counteroffensive of the Red Army. Overlord refers to the Normandy landings in 1944.

cau_hoi: The Allied evacuation by sea in 1940 took place at which beach in France?
giai_thich: In May 1940, British and French troops were pushed back to the port of Dunkirk by German forces. From May 26 to June 4, about 338,000 soldiers were evacuated to Britain by warships along with hundreds of fishing boats and private yachts, referred to as "the little ships." The British called this the "Dunkirk miracle," although Churchill reminded that "wars are not won by evacuations."

cau_hoi: What is the name of the act in 1707 that united England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain?
giai_thich: England and Scotland shared a king since 1603, when James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne and became James I. However, the two countries still had separate parliaments. In 1707, the Act of Union united the two countries into the Kingdom of Great Britain with a common parliament in London. Ireland joined in 1801.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the air battle in 1940 between the Royal Air Force and the German Air Force?
giai_thich: From July to October 1940, the German Air Force (Luftwaffe) sought to destroy the Royal Air Force (RAF) to pave the way for an invasion of Britain. The RAF won thanks to the Spitfire and Hurricane aircraft along with the radar system. Churchill praised the pilots: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few." Blitz refers to the bombing campaign of British cities that followed.

cau_hoi: Which city in the Soviet Union was besieged by German forces for nearly 900 days (1941 – 1944)?
giai_thich: From September 1941 to January 1944, for about 872 days, Leningrad was besieged by German forces. Approximately 1 million civilians died, mainly from starvation and cold. Supplies were only brought in through the "Road of Life" across the frozen Lake Ladoga. The city never surrendered, and in 1991 it regained its old name, Saint Petersburg.

cau_hoi: Where did the largest tank battle in history take place in 1943?
giai_thich: In July 1943, Germany launched Operation Citadel to attack the Kursk salient. The Soviet Union was aware of the plan and prepared multiple defensive lines. About 6,000 tanks from both sides participated, with the most famous battle being Prokhorovka. After this battle, Germany no longer had the strength to launch major offensives on the Eastern Front.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the U.S. aid plan for the reconstruction of Western Europe after World War II?
giai_thich: U.S. Secretary of State George Marshall proposed the plan in 1947. From 1948, the U.S. provided about $13 billion (equivalent to over $150 billion today) to Western European countries for reconstruction. The U.S. wanted Europe to recover quickly to prevent it from falling under Soviet influence. The Soviet Union forbade Eastern European countries from receiving this aid. Marshall was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1953.

cau_hoi: In which famous speech did Winston Churchill use the phrase "Iron Curtain"?
giai_thich: On March 5, 1946, at a university in Fulton, Missouri (USA), Churchill, who was no longer Prime Minister, stated that "an iron curtain has descended across the continent," from the Baltic Sea to the Adriatic Sea. This phrase described the division of Europe into a free West and an East under Soviet influence. It is often considered one of the key moments marking the beginning of the Cold War.

cau_hoi: How was the Soviet blockade of West Berlin (1948 – 1949) broken?
giai_thich: In June 1948, the Soviet Union blocked all road and rail access to West Berlin, which was located in East Germany. The U.S. and Britain organized an airlift, with planes landing approximately every minute, delivering coal, milk, and flour to about 2 million people. After nearly 11 months, the Soviet Union lifted the blockade. One pilot even dropped candy with small parachutes for children, earning the nickname "Candy Bomber."

cau_hoi: What was the name of the military alliance established by the Soviet Union in 1955?
giai_thich: In 1955, shortly after West Germany joined NATO, the Soviet Union established the Warsaw Pact with 7 Eastern European countries, signed in the Polish capital of Warsaw. This alliance served as NATO's military counterpart during the Cold War and was dissolved in 1991. COMECON was an economic organization, not a military alliance.

cau_hoi: What organization was established by the Treaty of Rome in 1957?
giai_thich: On March 25, 1957, six countries—France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg—signed the Treaty of Rome, establishing the European Economic Community (EEC), or "Common Market." The countries eliminated tariffs among themselves to facilitate trade. The EEC is the predecessor of the European Union, which was established in 1993.

cau_hoi: Which treaty signed in 1992 established the European Union (EU)?
giai_thich: The Maastricht Treaty was signed in February 1992 in the city of Maastricht, Netherlands, and came into effect on November 1, 1993. The treaty established the European Union, set forth European citizenship rights, and outlined the path to a common currency, the euro. The Lisbon Treaty in 2007 later reformed the functioning of the EU.

cau_hoi: In which country was the 1956 uprising against Soviet influence suppressed?
giai_thich: In October 1956, students and workers in Hungary protested for freedom and demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Prime Minister Imre Nagy declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact. In early November, Soviet tanks entered Budapest to suppress the uprising, resulting in thousands of deaths, around 200,000 people fleeing abroad, and Nagy later being executed.

cau_hoi: In which country did the "Prague Spring" of 1968 occur?
giai_thich: In 1968, Czechoslovak leader Alexander Dubček initiated reforms to create "socialism with a human face," easing censorship and allowing freedom of speech. In August 1968, about 250,000 troops from the Warsaw Pact entered the country to end the reforms. In 1969, student Jan Palach self-immolated in protest.

cau_hoi: In which country was the trade union "Solidarity" led by Lech Wałęsa founded?
giai_thich: In 1980, workers at the Gdańsk shipyard went on strike and established the independent trade union Solidarność, led by electrician Lech Wałęsa. This was the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc, with membership reaching up to 10 million at one point. In 1989, Solidarność won the semi-free elections. Wałęsa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 and became the President of Poland in 1990.

cau_hoi: "Velvet Revolution" in 1989 took place in which country?
giai_thich: In November 1989, after police beat students protesting in Prague, hundreds of thousands took to the streets, ringing keys as if to say "it's time to go home" to the government. Within weeks, the government relinquished power with almost no bloodshed, hence it is called the Velvet Revolution. Playwright Václav Havel became president.

cau_hoi: Which Soviet leader introduced the policies of "glasnost" (openness) and "perestroika" (restructuring)?
giai_thich: Mikhail Gorbachev became the leader of the Soviet Union in 1985. Glasnost (openness) allowed criticism and honest discussion of social issues. Perestroika (restructuring) aimed to renew the economy. He also did not intervene when Eastern European countries changed regimes in 1989. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990 and resigned when the Soviet Union dissolved at the end of 1991.

cau_hoi: In what year did Germany reunify?
giai_thich: On October 3, 1990, the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) merged with the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), less than a year after the fall of the Berlin Wall. The four victorious countries of World War II (the USA, the Soviet Union, the UK, and France) had signed a prior agreement. October 3 is Germany's National Day, and Berlin became the capital again.

cau_hoi: When did Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia?
giai_thich: After the Velvet Revolution, the Slovaks wanted their own state. The leaders of both sides agreed to a peaceful separation without a referendum. From January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia became two countries: the Czech Republic (capital Prague) and Slovakia (capital Bratislava). Due to the smooth separation process, the event is called the "Velvet Divorce."

cau_hoi: Which country officially left the European Union in 2020?
giai_thich: In the June 2016 referendum, about 52% of British voters chose to leave the EU. After several years of negotiations, the United Kingdom officially left the EU on January 31, 2020. "Brexit" is a portmanteau of "Britain" and "exit." Norway has never been an EU member, so it cannot be the answer.

cau_hoi: In 1961, which government ordered the construction of the Berlin Wall?
giai_thich: From 1949 to 1961, about 2.5 to 3 million East Germans fled to the West, many of whom were engineers and doctors. On the night of August 12-13, 1961, the East German government, with the approval of the Soviet Union, erected a barbed wire fence and then built a concrete wall about 155 km long around West Berlin. About 140 people died trying to cross the wall.

cau_hoi: Who was the first female Prime Minister of the United Kingdom?
giai_thich: Margaret Thatcher, the daughter of a grocery store owner, was a chemist before entering politics. She served as Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, the longest in the UK in the 20th century. A Soviet journalist nicknamed her "The Iron Lady" due to her tough stance. Theresa May (2016) and Liz Truss (2022) were later female Prime Ministers.

cau_hoi: Which city was besieged the longest in modern European warfare (1992 – 1996)?
giai_thich: When Yugoslavia disintegrated, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from April 1992 to February 1996, totaling 1,425 days. This was the longest siege of a capital in modern warfare. Residents had to run through intersections to avoid sniper fire. Ironically, Sarajevo had hosted the Winter Olympics in 1984.

cau_hoi: What is the period of Greek culture expansion following the conquests of Alexander the Great called?
giai_thich: After Alexander's death in 323 BC, his generals divided the empire and established kingdoms such as the Ptolemaic dynasty in Egypt and the Seleucid dynasty in Western Asia. Greek culture and language spread throughout the Mediterranean and Western Asia, hence it is called the Hellenistic period. The largest center was Alexandria with its famous Library of Alexandria. This period ended when Cleopatra was defeated at Actium in 31 BC.

cau_hoi: Which Bronze Age civilization developed on the island of Crete with the palace of Knossos?
giai_thich: The Minoans lived on the island of Crete from around 3000 to 1100 BC. They built the multi-story palace of Knossos with hundreds of rooms, including a water system, and painted vibrant frescoes such as scenes of bull-leaping. The name is derived from King Minos, who in mythology kept the Minotaur in a labyrinth. Their script, known as Linear A, remains undeciphered to this day.

cau_hoi: Which civilization developed in the region of Tuscany (Italy) before Rome rose to power?
giai_thich: The Etruscans lived in the region of Etruria (modern-day Tuscany) and thrived around the 8th to 5th centuries BC. Some of the first kings of Rome were Etruscan. The Romans learned many things from them: the arch, the art of augury, and even gladiatorial games. The name of the region 'Tuscany' is derived from this people.

cau_hoi: According to legend, who founded the city of Rome in 753 BC?
giai_thich: According to legend, Romulus and Remus were twin brothers, sons of the god of war Mars. The two brothers were abandoned in the Tiber River, suckled by a she-wolf, and raised by a shepherd. When founding the city, the brothers quarreled, and Romulus killed Remus, thus the city was named 'Roma' after him. The statue of the she-wolf nursing the two babies is a symbol of Rome.

cau_hoi: What form of government did the Romans transition to after overthrowing the king in 509 BC?
giai_thich: Traditionally, in 509 BC, the Romans expelled the arrogant king Tarquin and established the Republic (res publica, meaning 'the public matter'). Power was shared between two annually elected consuls and the Senate. The Romans hated the title 'king' so much that later emperors also avoided calling themselves kings.

cau_hoi: What are the two highest officials of the Roman Republic, elected each year, called?
giai_thich: Each year, Rome elected two consuls, who had equal power and could veto each other. This system prevented anyone from becoming a king. Their term lasted only one year. In times of great crisis, Rome would appoint a 'dictator' with full power for a maximum of 6 months. The Romans also recorded the year by the names of the two consuls of that year.

cau_hoi: Who led the largest slave revolt in Rome (73 – 71 BC)?
giai_thich: Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator. In 73 BC, he escaped from a gladiatorial school in Capua with about 70 gladiators, then gathered around 70,000 – 120,000 slaves. They defeated several Roman armies before being suppressed by Crassus in 71 BC. About 6,000 were crucified along the Appian Way as a warning.

cau_hoi: Which Gallic leader surrendered to Julius Caesar at Alesia in 52 BC?
giai_thich: Vercingetorix united the Gallic tribes against Caesar in 52 BC. Surrounded in the city of Alesia, he surrendered when Caesar built two walls: one facing the city and another facing outward to block reinforcements. He was taken to Rome and executed after 6 years of imprisonment. Today, he is regarded as the first national hero of France.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9, which German leader destroyed three Roman legions?
giai_thich: In AD 9, Arminius, a German leader who had served in the Roman army, led three Roman legions of General Varus into the Teutoburg Forest, ambushing and destroying about 15,000 – 20,000 soldiers. Emperor Augustus lamented, 'Varus, give me back my legions!' From then on, Rome considered the Rhine River as its border, preventing the Romanization of German lands.

cau_hoi: Who were the members of the First Triumvirate consisting of Julius Caesar, Pompey, and whom?
giai_thich: Around 60 BC, the three most powerful men in Rome secretly allied: Julius Caesar (a popular politician), Pompey (a renowned general), and Crassus (the richest man in Rome). The alliance broke apart when Crassus was killed at Carrhae in 53 BC during a battle against the Parthians. Afterwards, Caesar and Pompey fought each other. Lepidus and Mark Antony were part of the Second Triumvirate.

cau_hoi: Who deposed the last Western Roman Emperor in 476?
giai_thich: Odoacer was a German leader in the Roman army. In 476, he deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus but did not declare himself emperor. Instead, he sent the crown to Constantinople and ruled Italy as a king. Later, Theodoric, the king of the Ostrogoths, defeated and killed Odoacer in 493.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the first written code of law of Rome (around 450 BC)?
giai_thich: Around 451 – 450 BC, the Roman commoners demanded that the laws be written down so that the nobles could not interpret them arbitrarily. The laws were inscribed on 12 bronze tablets and placed in the Forum for everyone to read. Roman children had to memorize these laws. The original tablets were destroyed when the Gauls sacked Rome around 390 BC.

cau_hoi: Which Athenian lawmaker had such harsh laws that the term "draconian" (harsh) in English originated from his name?
giai_thich: Around 621 BC, Draco wrote the first written code of laws for Athens. The laws were so severe that even the theft of vegetables could be punishable by death. It is said that Draco's laws "were written in blood, not ink." Later, Solon abolished most of these laws, retaining only the law concerning murder.

cau_hoi: In Athens, what was the voting method using pottery shards to exile a politician for 10 years called?
giai_thich: Each year, Athenian citizens could vote on whether to exile someone by inscribing that person's name on a broken pottery shard (ostrakon).
