If there were 6,000 votes or more, the person with the most votes had to leave Athens for 10 years without losing their property. The purpose was to prevent anyone from becoming a tyrant. The term "ostracism" in modern English means "to boycott."

cau_hoi: Which Athenian general commanded the naval victory at Salamis in 480 BC?
giai_thich: Themistocles persuaded the Athenians to use money from a newly discovered silver mine to build about 200 triremes. In 480 BC, he lured the larger Persian fleet into the narrow strait of Salamis, where the Persian ships could not maneuver and were defeated. Ironically, he was later exiled from Athens and eventually lived in Persia.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the dense infantry formation with the long spear sarissa used by the Macedonians?
giai_thich: The phalanx is an infantry formation arranged in multiple closely packed rows. King Philip II of Macedonia, the father of Alexander, equipped his soldiers with the sarissa, a spear about 5 to 6 meters long, twice the length of a regular spear. The first five rows of spears pointed forward created a "wall of spikes" that was very difficult to break through. This formation helped Alexander conquer Persia.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the "tortoise" formation with shields closely packed used by the Romans?
giai_thich: In the testudo formation ("tortoise" in Latin), Roman soldiers in the outer rows held their shields in front and on the sides, while those in the middle held their shields overhead. The entire group resembled a turtle shell, providing protection from arrows and stones as they approached the city walls. This formation was slow and difficult for close combat, so it was only used when advancing under fire.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC, which famous tactic did Hannibal employ?
giai_thich: At Cannae (216 BC), Hannibal intentionally weakened the center of his formation and gradually retreated, luring the Roman forces to advance. Then, his strong infantry and cavalry closed in from both sides and the rear, completely encircling the Roman army. About 50,000 Roman soldiers died in just one day. This is a classic example of the "double envelopment" tactic.

cau_hoi: Which Roman general defeated Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC?
giai_thich: Instead of confronting Hannibal in Italy, Scipio took his army to attack Carthage directly in Africa, forcing Hannibal to return to defend it. In 202 BC at Zama, Scipio used drums to panic the war elephants and opened a path for them to run through his formation, then defeated Hannibal. He was awarded the title "Africanus." Fabius Maximus was known for his strategy of attrition, avoiding direct confrontation with Hannibal.

cau_hoi: In what year was the city of Carthage completely destroyed by the Romans?
giai_thich: After the Third Punic War, in 146 BC, Roman forces completely destroyed Carthage and sold its people into slavery. There is a story that they sprinkled salt on the land so nothing would grow, but historians believe this is a later fabrication. In the same year, Rome also destroyed the city of Corinth and took control of Greece.

cau_hoi: What was the main language used in the Byzantine Empire?
giai_thich: Initially, the Byzantine Empire used Latin in law and the military. However, most of the population in the east spoke Greek, so from the time of Emperor Heraclius (7th century), Greek became the official language. This helped preserve ancient Greek works, which were later brought to Italy and contributed to the Renaissance.

cau_hoi: Which empire possessed the secret weapon "Greek Fire" that could burn even on water?
giai_thich: "Greek Fire" was a flammable liquid sprayed through tubes from Byzantine ships, capable of burning even on water and very difficult to extinguish. This weapon helped Constantinople defeat the besieging Arab fleets in the 7th and 8th centuries. The formula was kept absolutely secret, known only to a few families, and has since been lost.

cau_hoi: Which Byzantine emperor was known as the "Bulgar Slayer"?
giai_thich: Basil II reigned for nearly 50 years (976 – 1025) and conquered the Bulgarian Empire. Legend has it that after the Battle of Kleidion in 1014, he had about 15,000 Bulgarian prisoners blinded, leaving one in every hundred with one eye to guide the others home. The King of Bulgaria reportedly died of heartbreak upon witnessing this.

cau_hoi: In which city did the Nika riots of 532 nearly overthrow Justinian?
giai_thich: In 532, the rival factions of chariot racers in Constantinople, the Greens and the Blues, who were traditionally enemies, united to riot, shouting "Nika!" (Victory!). They burned half the city, including the old Hagia Sophia. Justinian considered fleeing, but Empress Theodora convinced him to stay. The army cornered the rioters in the Hippodrome and suppressed them brutally.

cau_hoi: Under whose reign did the Rus in Kiev convert to Christianity in 988?
giai_thich: According to chronicles, Grand Duke Vladimir I of Kiev sent envoys to explore various religions. He chose Orthodoxy after hearing about the magnificent beauty of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. In 988, he had the people of Kiev baptized in the Dnieper River. This choice linked Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus to Byzantine culture.

cau_hoi: According to legend, which Viking leader founded the first state of the Rus in 862?
giai_thich: According to the "Primary Chronicle", in 862, Slavic tribes invited Rurik, a Varangian (Swedish Viking) leader, to rule Novgorod. His successor, Oleg, captured Kiev and established the Kievan Rus state. The Rurik dynasty ruled until 1598. The term "Rus", the root of the name Russia, may originate from the name of these Vikings.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the Mongol khanate that ruled the Rus lands from the 13th to the 15th century?
giai_thich: The Golden Horde was established by Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, after the Mongol conquest of the Rus principalities around 1237 – 1240. The Rus princes had to pay tribute and seek the khan's favor for titles. This period is referred to by Russians as the "Tatar Yoke", lasting until 1480. The Yuan Dynasty was also established by Mongols, but in China.

cau_hoi: Which Russian prince defeated the Teutonic Knights on the frozen Lake Peipus in 1242?
giai_thich: In 1242, the Teutonic Knights (Germans) attacked the Novgorod region. Prince Alexander Nevsky lured them onto the frozen Lake Peipus, located between present-day Russia and Estonia, and defeated them. Legend has it that the ice broke under the weight of the knights' armor. Director Eisenstein made a film about this battle in 1938. Nevsky was canonized by the Russian Orthodox Church.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380, the Russian forces defeated the Golden Horde under whose command?
giai_thich: In 1380, Grand Duke Dmitry of Moscow led a coalition of Russian principalities to defeat the Golden Horde on the Kulikovo Field, near the Don River. He is referred to as Donskoy ("of the Don"). Although the Russians had to continue paying tribute for another 100 years, this victory proved that the Mongols were not invincible and elevated Moscow's status.

cau_hoi: Who was the first to officially be crowned with the title "Tsar" in 1547?
giai_thich: Ivan IV's grandfather, Ivan III, occasionally used the title "Tsar", but in 1547, Ivan IV, at just 16 years old, was the first to be officially crowned as "Tsar of All Russia". The term "Tsar" originates from "Caesar". He earned the nickname "the Terrible" (Grozny), which originally meant "formidable", due to his brutal purges.

cau_hoi: The Romanov dynasty began in 1613 with which tsar?
giai_thich: After the "Time of Troubles" (1598 – 1613), when Russia had no official tsar and was occupied by Poland, a national assembly elected Mikhail Romanov, who was only 16 at the time, as tsar. The Romanov dynasty ruled Russia for over 300 years until Nicholas II abdicated in 1917. Peter the Great was Mikhail's grandson.

cau_hoi: The Kalmar Union of 1397 united which three kingdoms under one king?
giai_thich: In 1397, in the city of Kalmar (Sweden), Queen Margaret I of Denmark united the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden, which then included Finland, under one king, her grandson Eric of Pomerania. This union formed one of the largest states in Europe, lasting until 1523 when Gustav Vasa separated Sweden.

cau_hoi: Which Swedish king was called the "Lion of the North" during the Thirty Years' War?
giai_thich: Gustavus Adolphus reformed the Swedish army with mobile light artillery and flexible units. He entered the Thirty Years' War in 1630 to protect the Protestant side and achieved many significant victories. He died at Lützen in 1632 while the Swedish forces still won that battle. He is known as the "Lion of the North" and the "Father of Modern Warfare."

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Poltava in 1709, which Swedish king was defeated by Peter the Great?
giai_thich: Charles XII was the young warrior king of Sweden, winning many battles during the Great Northern War. In 1708, he advanced deep into Russia, but his army was exhausted by the harshest winter of the century. In 1709 at Poltava (now in Ukraine), he was defeated by Peter the Great and had to flee to the Ottoman Empire. This victory elevated Russia to a Northern European power in place of Sweden.

cau_hoi: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was officially formed in 1569 through which union?
giai_thich: In 1385, the Union of Krewo linked Poland and Lithuania through the marriage of Queen Jadwiga and Grand Duke Jogaila, but the two countries remained separate. By 1569, the Union of Lublin merged them into a federal state with a common elected king and parliament. At its height, it was one of the largest countries in Europe.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, the Polish-Lithuanian alliance defeated which forces?
giai_thich: The Teutonic Knights were a German military order that occupied many areas along the Baltic coast. On July 15, 1410, the Polish-Lithuanian alliance led by King Władysław II Jagiełło defeated them at Grunwald (Tannenberg). The Grand Master of the order was killed. This battle ended the eastward expansion of the Teutonic Knights.

cau_hoi: Which Polish king relieved the siege of Vienna from the Ottoman forces in 1683?
giai_thich: In 1683, about 150,000 Ottoman troops besieged Vienna for the second time. Polish King Jan III Sobieski led the coalition to rescue it. On September 12, 1683, he commanded about 18,000 cavalry, most notably the Polish winged hussars with wings attached to their backs, charging down the hill to attack. The Ottoman forces were shattered. This is considered the largest cavalry charge in history.

cau_hoi: Which Ottoman Sultan besieged Vienna for the first time in 1529?
giai_thich: Suleiman I ruled from 1520 to 1566, during the peak of the Ottoman Empire, which stretched from Hungary to Arabia. In 1529, he besieged Vienna but had to withdraw due to an early winter and long supply lines. The West called him "the Magnificent," while the Turks referred to him as "Kanuni" (the Lawgiver) because of his legal reforms.

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Mohács in 1526, the Ottoman forces defeated which kingdom?
giai_thich: On August 29, 1526, the Ottoman forces of Suleiman defeated the Hungarian army at Mohács. King Louis II of Hungary, only 20 years old, drowned while fleeing across a stream. Since he had no heirs, the Hungarian throne fell to the Habsburgs, while much of Hungary was occupied by the Ottomans for about 150 years.

cau_hoi: The Battle of Kosovo in 1389 was a confrontation between the Ottomans and which forces?
giai_thich: On June 28, 1389, the Serbian forces led by Prince Lazar clashed with the Ottoman army at the Field of Blackbirds (Kosovo). Both leaders died: Lazar was killed in battle, while Sultan Murad I was stabbed to death by a Serbian knight. The battle became legendary in Serbian culture. Coincidentally, the assassination in Sarajevo in 1914 also occurred on the anniversary of June 28.

cau_hoi: Which prince of Wallachia inspired the character Dracula?
giai_thich: Vlad III ruled Wallachia (now part of Romania) in the 15th century and resisted the Ottomans. He was notorious for his brutality, impaling thousands of enemies on sharp stakes, earning the nickname "the Impaler." His father was part of the Order of the Dragon ("Dracul"), so he was called "Dracula," meaning son of Dracul. In 1897, Irish author Bram Stoker borrowed this name for his famous vampire character.

cau_hoi: Which national hero of Albania fought against the Ottomans in the 15th century?
giai_thich: Skanderbeg (real name Gjergj Kastrioti) was once a hostage and officer in the Ottoman army. In 1443, he escaped back to Albania and led a resistance for 25 years, defeating many larger Ottoman armies. His family's red flag with a double-headed black eagle is now the national flag of Albania. The name "Skanderbeg" means "Lord Alexander."

cau_hoi: In the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, which navy was defeated by the Holy League?
giai_thich: On October 7, 1571, the fleet of the Holy League, consisting of Spain, Venice, and the Pope, commanded by Don Juan of Austria, defeated the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Lepanto, Greece. This was the last major naval battle primarily using rowing ships, with over 400 vessels involved. The writer Cervantes, author of 'Don Quixote', was wounded and lost the use of his left hand in this battle.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the Dutch war for independence from Spain (1568 – 1648)?
giai_thich: The Protestant provinces of the Netherlands rebelled against King Philip II of Spain, a Catholic who imposed heavy taxes. The war lasted from 1568 to 1648, a total of 80 years, with a 12-year truce in between. During this time, the Netherlands became a wealthy trading power, known as the 'Dutch Golden Age'. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 recognized Dutch independence.

cau_hoi: Who initiated the Dutch uprising against Spain, nicknamed 'The Silent'?
giai_thich: William of Orange (1533 – 1584) was a wealthy nobleman and the leader of the Dutch uprising. The nickname 'The Silent' is believed to be due to his ability to keep plans secret. He was assassinated in 1584, becoming one of the first heads of state to be killed by a handgun. The Dutch national anthem 'Wilhelmus' is written about him, and the orange color of the Dutch national team comes from the House of Orange.

cau_hoi: In what year was the Dutch East India Company (VOC), considered the first publicly traded company, established?
giai_thich: The VOC was established in 1602 to trade spices in Asia, particularly Indonesia. To raise capital, the company sold shares to anyone, and the shares were traded in Amsterdam, which had the world's earliest stock exchange. The VOC had its own army, warships, and the right to sign treaties. The British East India Company was established earlier in 1600 but did not initially issue shares in this manner.

cau_hoi: The War of Spanish Succession (1701 – 1714) ended with which treaty?
giai_thich: When King Charles II of Spain died in 1700 without an heir, he bequeathed the throne to Philip, the grandson of King Louis XIV of France. Other countries feared that a union of France and Spain would be too powerful, leading to war. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 allowed Philip V to keep the throne on the condition that the two kingdoms would never unite. Britain gained Gibraltar and Minorca.

cau_hoi: In what year did the Seven Years' War end with the Treaty of Paris?
giai_thich: The Seven Years' War (1756 – 1763) is considered the first 'world war' as it took place in Europe, North America, India, and across the oceans. The Treaty of Paris in 1763 ceded Canada and the eastern part of the Mississippi River to Britain, while France lost nearly all its colonies in North America. Note that 1783 refers to another Treaty of Paris that recognized the independence of the United States.

cau_hoi: The 'Brandenburg Miracle' in 1762 that saved Prussia occurred due to the death of whom?
giai_thich: In 1762, Frederick the Great's Prussia was on the verge of defeat against the Russian, Austrian, and French alliance. Just then, Empress Elizabeth of Russia died. Her successor, Peter III, who greatly admired Frederick, signed a peace treaty and returned the occupied lands. Frederick called this the 'Brandenburg Miracle'. A few months later, Peter III was overthrown by his own wife, Catherine (the Great).

cau_hoi: Which estate's representatives took the 'Tennis Court Oath' in 1789?
giai_thich: At that time, France had three estates: clergy, nobility, and the third estate, which consisted of commoners, making up about 97% of the population. In June 1789, locked out of the meeting room, the representatives of the third estate moved to an indoor tennis court (jeu de paume) in Versailles. There, they swore not to disband until they had written a constitution. This was a significant step before the storming of the Bastille.

cau_hoi: On the 18th of Brumaire in Year VIII of the French Revolutionary Calendar, what did Napoleon do?
giai_thich: The French Revolution used a unique calendar with months named after weather conditions, such as Brumaire meaning 'month of fog'. On the 18th of Brumaire in Year VIII (November 9, 1799), Napoleon staged a coup to overthrow the Directory and became the First Consul, seizing full power. Five years later, he proclaimed himself emperor. The phrase '18 Brumaire' today refers to a coup d'état.

cau_hoi: In what year did Napoleon proclaim himself emperor?
giai_thich: In 1804, after a referendum, Napoleon became the Emperor of the French. On December 2, 1804, at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris, he took the crown from Pope Pius VII and placed it on his own head, to demonstrate that his power did not come from the Church. The painter Jacques-Louis David depicted the coronation in a monumental painting.

cau_hoi: When was the Holy Roman Empire officially dissolved?
giai_thich: After Napoleon defeated Austria and established the "Rhine Confederation" consisting of German states, Emperor Francis II declared the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire on August 6, 1806, ending an empire that had existed for about 844 years since the time of Otto I. He retained the title of Emperor of Austria, taking the name Francis I.

cau_hoi: What was Napoleon's "Continental System" aimed at?
giai_thich: In 1806, Napoleon was unable to defeat the British navy, so he prohibited all European countries under his control from trading with Britain, hoping to collapse the British economy. However, Europe itself lacked goods and smuggling was rampant. When Russia refused to comply, Napoleon invaded Russia in 1812, a decision that led to his downfall.

cau_hoi: What is the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 also known as?
giai_thich: In October 1813, near the city of Leipzig (Germany), about 500,000 to 600,000 soldiers from France, Russia, Prussia, Austria, Sweden, and various German states clashed. This was the largest battle in Europe until World War I. Due to the many nations involved, it was called the "Battle of Nations." Napoleon was defeated and had to retreat to France, and the following year he abdicated.

cau_hoi: Who commanded the British and allied forces at the Battle of Waterloo?
giai_thich: Arthur Wellesley, the Duke of Wellington, had defeated French forces multiple times in Spain. At Waterloo in 1815, his troops held out against Napoleon's assaults until the Prussian forces led by Field Marshal Blücher arrived to assist in the evening. Wellington remarked that it was "the closest-run thing you ever saw." He later became the Prime Minister of Britain. The rubber boots "Wellington boots" are named after him.

cau_hoi: Which French emperor was captured at Sedan during the Franco-Prussian War in 1870?
giai_thich: In 1870, France declared war on Prussia, just as Bismarck had hoped. On September 2, 1870, at Sedan, Emperor Napoleon III was surrounded and surrendered along with over 100,000 soldiers. Two days later, Paris declared the Third Republic. Napoleon III was the nephew of Napoleon Bonaparte. He lived in exile in England until his death in 1873.

cau_hoi: What was the revolutionary government that took power in Paris in 1871 called?
giai_thich: After France's defeat by Prussia, the people of Paris rejected the new government that signed the peace treaty. In March 1871, they established the Paris Commune, self-governing the city, separating church from state, and banning night shifts in bakeries. After about 72 days, government troops retook Paris in the "Bloody Week," resulting in tens of thousands of deaths.

cau_hoi: The Seven Weeks' War in 1866 was a conflict between Prussia and which country?
giai_thich: In 1866, Bismarck waged war against Austria to gain leadership over the German states. By using railroads to transport troops and breech-loading rifles, the Prussian army quickly won at the Battle of Königgrätz (Sadowa). The war lasted only about 7 weeks. Austria was excluded from the process of German unification, and Prussia established the North German Confederation.

cau_hoi: Which English poet died in 1824 while participating in the Greek War of Independence?
giai_thich: Lord Byron was the most famous romantic poet in England at the time and had a deep love for ancient Greek culture. In 1823, he used his own money to equip the Greek army fighting against the Ottomans. In 1824, he fell ill and died in Missolonghi at the age of 36. The Greeks regarded him as a national hero, and many streets in Greece are named after him.

cau_hoi: The secret organization "Black Hand," involved in the assassination in 1914, was made up of nationalists from which country?
giai_thich: "Black Hand" (officially "Unity or Death") was a secret society founded by Serbian army officers in 1911, led by Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević (alias Apis). They aimed to unify lands with Serbian populations, including Bosnia, which was under Austro-Hungarian control. The society provided weapons and training to the group of young men who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand.

cau_hoi: Who shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914?
giai_thich: On the morning of June 28, 1914, Čabrinović threw a grenade at the Archduke's convoy but missed. In the afternoon, the Archduke's driver took a wrong turn and stopped the car right in front of Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old standing near a bakery. Princip shot and killed the Archduke and his wife. Because he was under 20 years old, Princip was not sentenced to death. He died in prison in 1918 from tuberculosis.

cau_hoi: In the Zimmermann Telegram of 1917, Germany proposed an alliance with which country against the United States?
giai_thich: In January 1917, German Foreign Minister Arthur Zimmermann sent a secret telegram to Mexico. Germany promised that if Mexico attacked the United States, it would help Mexico regain Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. British intelligence decrypted the telegram and passed it to the U.S. When the telegram was made public, American public opinion was outraged, and in April 1917, the U.S. declared war on Germany.

cau_hoi: Where did the Easter Rising of 1916 take place?
giai_thich: During Easter in April 1916, about 1,600 Irish nationalists occupied buildings in Dublin, such as the General Post Office, and declared the Irish Republic. British forces suppressed the uprising after six days and executed 16 leaders. The executions further galvanized Irish support for independence. In 1922, most of Ireland became the Irish Free State.

cau_hoi: The Battle of Jutland in 1916, the largest naval battle of World War I, was a confrontation between Britain and which country?
giai_thich: From May 31 to June 1, 1916, the British fleet (Grand Fleet) clashed with the German fleet (High Seas Fleet) off the coast of Jutland, Denmark. Britain lost more ships and men, but Germany did not dare to send its large fleet to sea again for the rest of the war. This was the only major naval battle between giant battleships in World War I.

cau_hoi: The Gallipoli Campaign of 1915 by the Allies aimed to control which strait?
giai_thich: The Dardanelles Strait connects the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara, on the way to Constantinople. In 1915, British Naval Minister Winston Churchill supported the plan to seize the strait to defeat the Ottomans and open a supply route to Russia. British, French, Australian, and New Zealand (ANZAC) troops landed on the Gallipoli Peninsula but were halted, suffering around 250,000 casualties on each side. April 25 is now ANZAC Day in Australia and New Zealand.

cau_hoi: Which founder of modern Turkey became famous for commanding at Gallipoli?
giai_thich: At Gallipoli in 1915, Colonel Mustafa Kemal commanded Ottoman forces to successfully block the Allies at key positions. After World War I, he led the independence struggle and established the Republic of Turkey in 1923. He implemented many significant reforms, such as adopting the Latin alphabet and granting women the right to vote. In 1934, the parliament awarded him the surname "Atatürk," meaning "Father of the Turks."

cau_hoi: Which treaty in 1920 caused Hungary to lose about two-thirds of its territory after World War I?
giai_thich: The Treaty of Trianon (June 4, 1920), signed at the Grand Trianon Palace in Versailles, caused Hungary to lose about 72% of its territory, with over 3 million Hungarians becoming citizens of Romania, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia. To this day, Hungarians still regard this as a national trauma. The Treaty of Saint-Germain was signed with Austria, while the Treaty of Neuilly was signed with Bulgaria.

cau_hoi: Which empire was the Treaty of Sèvres signed with in 1920?
giai_thich: The Treaty of Sèvres (1920) fragmented the Ottoman Empire: Arab regions were handed over to British and French control, while parts of Anatolia were given to Greece, Italy, and Armenia. The Turks, under Mustafa Kemal's leadership, rejected this and fought to reclaim their land. In 1923, the Treaty of Lausanne replaced Sèvres and recognized the new borders of Turkey as they are today.

cau_hoi: The Locarno Treaty of 1925 confirmed Germany's western borders with which countries?
giai_thich: In 1925, at Locarno (Switzerland), Germany agreed to respect its borders with France and Belgium while keeping the Rhineland as a demilitarized zone. The treaty created a "Locarno spirit" of optimism for peace, and the following year Germany was admitted to the League of Nations. However, the eastern borders with Poland and Czechoslovakia were not guaranteed similarly. In 1936, Hitler violated the treaty by sending troops into the Rhineland.

cau_hoi: Where did Hitler's "Beer Hall Putsch" of 1923 take place?
giai_thich: In November 1923, Hitler and the Nazi Party attempted a coup at a large beer hall in Munich, intending to march on Berlin from there. The coup was suppressed by the police within a day. Hitler was sentenced to five years in prison but served only about nine months. While in prison, he wrote "Mein Kampf" (My Struggle). He later shifted to seeking power through elections.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the republic in Germany from 1919 to 1933?
giai_thich: After Emperor Wilhelm II abdicated in 1918, Germany became a republic. The new constitution was drafted in 1919 in the city of Weimar, rather than chaotic Berlin, hence it was called the Weimar Republic. This republic faced hyperinflation in 1923, when the price of a loaf of bread soared to billions of marks, followed by the Great Depression. Hitler became Chancellor in 1933, ending the republic.

cau_hoi: What are the names of the two foreign ministers who signed the non-aggression pact between Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939?
giai_thich: On August 23, 1939, Soviet Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov and German Foreign Minister Joachim von Ribbentrop signed a pact committing not to attack each other for 10 years. The secret clauses divided Poland, the Baltic states, and Finland into spheres of influence for each side. A week later, Germany invaded Poland. Nearly two years later, Hitler broke the pact by invading the Soviet Union.

cau_hoi: "Winter War" 1939 – 1940 was a conflict between the Soviet Union and which country?
giai_thich: In November 1939, the Soviet Union attacked Finland to claim land near Leningrad. The Finnish forces were significantly outnumbered but wore white camouflage and moved on skis, inflicting heavy damage on the Red Army in temperatures that sometimes dropped to -40°C. By March 1940, Finland had to cede about 10% of its territory but still maintained its independence. This war also gave rise to the term "Molotov cocktail" for a type of homemade incendiary device.

cau_hoi: Which French Marshal led the Vichy government that collaborated with Germany?
giai_thich: After France's defeat by Germany in June 1940, Marshal Philippe Pétain, a hero of the Battle of Verdun in 1916 and at that time 84 years old, established a government in the spa town of Vichy and collaborated with Nazi Germany. Charles de Gaulle went to London and led the "Free French" resistance movement. After the war, Pétain was sentenced to death, but his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the airborne operation in 1944 in the Netherlands, which failed at Arnhem?
giai_thich: In September 1944, British Marshal Montgomery launched Operation Market Garden: paratroopers (the "Market" part) jumped in to capture bridges in the Netherlands, while tanks (the "Garden" part) advanced along the road connecting the bridges. The goal was to cross the Rhine River and end the war before Christmas. British paratroopers at Arnhem were surrounded, and the last bridge could not be held. The film "A Bridge Too Far" recounts this operation.

cau_hoi: What was the name of the Soviet summer campaign in 1944 that shattered the German Army Group Center?
giai_thich: In June 1944, exactly three years after Germany attacked the Soviet Union and just two weeks after the Normandy landings, the Red Army launched Operation Bagration in Belarus. The operation destroyed nearly the entire German Army Group Center, causing Germany to lose hundreds of thousands of soldiers, more than at Stalingrad. The operation was named after General Pyotr Bagration, who died at Borodino in 1812. Uranus was the operation that encircled Stalingrad, while Citadel was the German offensive at Kursk.

cau_hoi: Where did Germany's last major counteroffensive on the Western Front (December 1944) take place?
giai_thich: On December 16, 1944, Hitler unexpectedly attacked through the Ardennes Forest (Belgium and Luxembourg), hoping to split the Allied forces and capture the port of Antwerp. The attack created a bulge in the front line, which the Americans called the "Battle of the Bulge." American troops in Bastogne were surrounded, but their general responded to the surrender proposal with just one word: "Nuts!" By January 1945, Germany was defeated.

cau_hoi: Who replaced Winston Churchill midway through the Potsdam Conference in 1945?
giai_thich: The Potsdam Conference (July – August 1945) discussed how to handle defeated Germany. Midway through the conference, the results of the election in Britain were announced: the Labour Party won decisively, so Clement Attlee replaced Churchill as Prime Minister and head of the British delegation. The U.S. also had a new leader, Harry Truman, as Roosevelt had died in April 1945. Only Stalin was present at both Yalta and Potsdam.

cau_hoi: In which city was the international tribunal that tried Nazi leaders (1945 – 1946) held?
giai_thich: From November 1945 to October 1946, the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg tried 24 Nazi leaders. This was the first time leaders were tried for crimes such as "crimes against humanity." 12 people were sentenced to death. Nuremberg was chosen because the court there was intact and because the city had previously been the site of large Nazi rallies.

cau_hoi: What community was proposed in the Schuman Declaration of 1950?
giai_thich: On May 9, 1950, French Foreign Minister Robert Schuman proposed placing the coal and steel industries of France and West Germany under a common authority. Coal and steel are essential materials for making weapons, so managing them together would make war between the two countries "impossible." In 1951, the European Coal and Steel Community was established with six countries. May 9 is now celebrated as Europe Day.

cau_hoi: In which country was the Schengen Agreement signed in 1985?
giai_thich: In 1985, the countries of France, West Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Luxembourg signed the agreement on a boat on the Moselle River, near the village of Schengen in Luxembourg, agreeing to gradually abolish passport checks at their common borders. The village is located at the point where Luxembourg, France, and Germany meet. Today, the Schengen area includes about 29 countries, allowing people to travel between these countries without needing to show a passport.

cau_hoi: Which Yugoslav leader firmly maintained independence from the Soviet Union after 1948?
giai_thich: Josip Broz Tito led the Yugoslav partisans to drive out German forces during World War II with little help from the Red Army. In 1948, he disagreed with Stalin and was expelled from the Cominform bloc, but Yugoslavia remained independent. In 1961, he, along with Nehru (India), Nasser (Egypt), and Sukarno (Indonesia), founded the Non-Aligned Movement. After his death in 1980, Yugoslavia gradually disintegrated.

cau_hoi: Which Romanian leader was executed in December 1989?
giai_thich: Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled Romania autocratically from 1965 and kept the population living in poverty to pay off foreign debts. In December 1989, protests erupted in Timișoara and spread to Bucharest, with the army turning to support the people. Ceaușescu and his wife fled, were captured, and quickly tried and executed on Christmas Day, December 25, 1989.

cau_hoi: Which playwright became the president of Czechoslovakia after 1989?
giai_thich: Václav Havel was a famous playwright who was imprisoned multiple times by the communist regime for fighting for human rights. After the Velvet Revolution, he was elected president of Czechoslovakia on December 29, 1989. From 1993, he became the first president of the Czech Republic and served until 2003. Prague Airport is now named after him.

cau_hoi: "The Baltic Way" in 1989 saw about 2 million people holding hands across which three countries?
giai_thich: On August 23, 1989, exactly 50 years after the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, which had handed the three Baltic states to the Soviet Union, about 2 million people joined hands to form a chain approximately 675 km long across Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. They demanded independence. This event was included in UNESCO's "Memory of the World" register. Lithuania declared independence in 1990, and all three countries were recognized in 1991.

cau_hoi: The agreement that ended the Bosnian War in 1995 was negotiated in which U.S. city?
giai_thich: In November 1995, the presidents of Bosnia, Serbia, and Croatia were invited by the U.S. to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio, where they negotiated for three weeks. The Dayton Agreement ended a war that claimed about 100,000 lives. Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided into two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Croatia and the Serb Republic. The agreement was officially signed in Paris in December 1995.

cau_hoi: The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 brought peace to which region?
giai_thich: Since the late 1960s, Northern Ireland experienced about 30 years of violence known as "The Troubles," between those wanting to remain part of the United Kingdom (mostly Protestant) and those wanting to merge with Ireland (mostly Catholic). About 3,500 people died. The agreement signed on Good Friday, April 10, 1998, established a power-sharing government between the two communities.

cau_hoi: The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 granted Britain which territory at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula?
giai_thich: Gibraltar is a small rock at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, controlling the strait connecting the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean. Britain captured Gibraltar in 1704, and the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 officially ceded the territory to Britain. Spain still claims it, but in referendums, the people of Gibraltar have chosen to remain with Britain. It is also famous for its unique population of wild monkeys in Europe.

cau_hoi: Which philosopher was burned at the stake in 1600 in which city?
giai_thich: Giordano Bruno was an Italian monk and philosopher. He believed in an infinite universe, that stars are other suns, and that there could be many worlds with life. He also held views contrary to the Church's doctrine. After 7 years of imprisonment and trial, he was burned at the stake by the Inquisition in Campo de' Fiori square, Rome, in 1600. A statue of him now stands there.

cau_hoi: What is the name of the decree from 1492 that expelled Jews from Spain?
giai_thich: On March 31, 1492, a few months after capturing Granada, King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella issued the decree at the Alhambra Palace. The decree forced Jews in Spain to convert to Catholicism or leave the country within four months. Tens of thousands had to depart, many to the Ottoman Empire. In 1968, Spain officially revoked this decree.

cau_hoi: Which French king issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598 granting religious freedom to Huguenots?
giai_thich: Henri IV was originally Protestant, but to be accepted as king by Catholic Parisians, he converted and is said to have remarked, "Paris is worth a mass." In 1598, he issued the Edict of Nantes granting French Protestants (Huguenots) the freedom to worship, ending over 30 years of religious wars. In 1685, Louis XIV revoked the edict, causing about 200,000 Huguenots to flee abroad.
